utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please. Not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-0 -- sorry, IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. Present for the Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Vanderpuye and Ms. Soljan; and from the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Josse, and Mr. Haynes. Now, I understand you have some preliminaries. We, too, have some preliminaries, so let's start from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. President, we had previously submitted a motion to amend the 65 ter exhibit list with respect to the witness that is now coming up. The Defence had filed a response to that motion. I don't know if you want us to argue this issue orally, but I think that there is a sufficient-enough basis in the record to grant the relief that's requested. In addition, we do have a witness that is following this upcoming witness who has a rather tight schedule in order to -- to accommodate, so I don't know if you want to entertain this issue now or you want to entertain it perhaps later on. But I could respond, if you would like, to the Defence arguments that have been raised in response to our motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the two positions, Mr. Vanderpuye, have been put very clearly in the written filings. Our position was last week that since Mr. Manning was due to testify today, we cut short or reduce the time limit for the filing of the Defence objections, and we made it clear, we believe, that anyone who wished to say anything or respond to your motion would have had to do that by the end of business last Friday. We have had filings, as you are aware. I think the position is pretty much clear in our minds, and I don't think that any further comments on your part will change anything. So you --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There was also a Defence submission regarding the scope of the testimony to be offered by Mr. Manning, which we also have responded to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, and the same thing applies to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was a time limit for you to respond. We don't think it's the case of hearing any further submissions. We are going to decide the two motions orally this morning before Mr. Manning comes in. That's number one. The other thing is last Friday, I think it was, we left you with the understanding that you would be continuing discussions amongst yourselves in relation to the notebooks, logbooks, and whatever the documents that were discussed very briefly last time. You were supposed to come back to us today, and we also were supposed to come back to you today after hearing your position, respective positions, whether you've come to an agreement or whether you still disagree, in which case we will tell you what will happen. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We all met on Friday and reached some agreements, but I think we're still in the discussion stage. But we're very close. I don't see -- if perhaps we can talk at the first break, I think we can iron things out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you. So we are seized of the following Defence motion requesting determination as to the admissibility of the evidence of Dean Manning. This was filed by the Popovic Defence team on the 5th of November. It was joint by the Nikolic Defence team, by the Beara Defence team, by the Borovcanin Defence team, and then we had a Prosecution response filed on the 7th of December. We've gone carefully through motions and main response, as well as the other filings joining in with the Popovic Defence team, and our decision is as follows: First of all, we have granted leave to the Popovic Defence team to exceed the word limit. We are hereby deciding to deny or reject the Popovic motion by stating, by affirming that Dean Manning's testimony should not be restricted as sought in that motion, particularly, although not exclusively, in the light of the quantity -- that in the light of the quantity and the complexity of the exhumations and associated documentation in this case, we consider, we believe that a witness who is able to provide a comparative overview on the basis of detailed knowledge, acquired over a period of time, will be of assistance to the Tribunal. However, we are also deciding that Mr. Manning should not testify in regard to any expert evidence which is not before the Trial Chamber. We also wish to make clear that the question of admissibility of any document to be tendered in the course of Mr. Manning's testimony will be addressed at the end of his testimony in accordance with established practice in this case. That disposes of that motion. Then there was a Prosecution motion for leave to amend the 65 ter exhibit list with exhibits pertaining to Witness number 2, that's Manning, which was filed confidentially on the 5th of December, 2007. Mr. Vanderpuye, even though this was filed confidentially, I think we can dispose of it publicly, can't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We've seen the Defence response, which was filed on the 7th of December, then there was a motion on behalf of Drago Nikolic joining the previous Defence response of the Popovic team, and also another one forthcoming from the Beara Defence team, and finally from the Borovcanin Defence team. We're talking of a motion to seek leave to add to the 65 ter list eight newly-received documents related to exhumations and numbers of the Srebrenica missing and identified dead people, six documents developed for demonstrative purposes, and the witness's 24th August 2003 report which was inadvertently omitted from the original 65 ter list. We agree with the Prosecution that all the proposed exhibits are prima facie relevant, and we also note that, with the exception of the Manning 2003 report, these were received by the Defence. They were received only in the last two months, and all the exhibits have been disclosed to the Defence. We are also satisfied that, at least on a prima facie basis, none of the material contains any information that in any way changes the nature of the Prosecution case or the substance of Mr. Manning's testimony. In going through the Popovic response, which has been joined by other Defence teams, as already stated, we notice that almost the entire list of objections raised go largely to the weight to be given to the exhibits rather than whether they should be added to the 65 ter list. However, we are not happy, Mr. McCloskey, with the way this has been progressing, and we are concerned particularly when it comes to voluminous material like we have in the present case. So in acceding to your motion, in granting the motion, we are also making a reservation for all the Defence teams, even those who have not filed a response, that considering the limited time that they have had available to go through all this material, should any one of them in due course feel the need to recall Mr. Manning for further cross-examination, we are making it clear that such a request, if good cause is shown by the respective Defence teams, such a request will be granted. Otherwise, the motion itself is being granted. I'm also making it clear that what the -- the caveat that I have mentioned applies mainly to the 15 exhibits that the motion refers to in the first place. All right. So that settles the two motions pending and responses pending before the testimony of Mr. Manning. Are there any other preliminary matters you wish to raise? Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Just a matter of clarification, perhaps. Apparently, Your Honours have decided that Mr. Manning shall not testify in regards to any expert evidence which is not before the Trial Chamber already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: However, then you granted the 65 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I haven't said "already." " MR. MEEK: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't said "already," which is not before the Trial Chamber. It could be forthcoming next week through another witness, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Well, one caveat, then, is that in the documents which you've just granted that can be admitted, for example, is a report, "Srebrenica Missing," done by the ICMP. That evidence is not before this Trial Chamber, nor do I believe there will be any experts called to discuss those issues. So my question would simply be: How can he -- how can this document come in through Manning if it's not before the Trial Chamber and is not going to be before the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If the Prosecution seeks to bring it in, introduce it into the records, you just stand up and raise it at the right time, and then we will deal with it at that moment; but, otherwise, I don't want to jump the gun now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we have decided is we haven't admitted any documents; we've just included the list that Mr. McCloskey indicated and the 65 ter list. Whether use is made of those documents or not is another matter. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The reference document is an updated version of our original 65 ter 566, but it's my understanding Mr. Manning will not be dealing with that specifically. That's a document that's assembled by our demographics people, and we've heard all about that already. This is an update, So I think we don't really have an issue there, as yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. No, this is what we meant. What we have decided is the introduction or inclusion of these documents in the 65 ter list. What's going to happen with them is another matter. And if there are objections as to admissibility, we'll deal with the admissibility issue when it arises. Okay? Anything else? Mr. Manning. Yes, one moment. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. We submitted a motion for permission of the Trial Chamber to -- for our military expert to be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. There are two Defence teams, Popovic and Nikolic Defence team, that would like to have their military expert present during the testimony of Richard Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objection. So the motions, Ms. Nikolic and Mr. Zivanovic, are hereby being granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Anything else, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, maybe we could have done this in a different manner, but I think it would be much simpler to do it orally. We would also like, I mean the Defence of Mr. Borovcanin, to have our expert witness present during the testimony of Mr. Butler, so maybe this is a good opportunity to make a decision about all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The United States would like to have a lawyer present during Mr. Butler, and maybe we can just get this all done very orally and save some paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe also, I mean, we'll come to this later on, but the idea of having -- you're, of course, entitled to it. But the idea of each Defence team having an expert of its own on a particular matter, if it is out-stretched, we will intervene, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- over-stretched, we will intervene. Yes. I think you need to file a proper, because we need to know why the American government, US government would like to have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They've always done it, and we'll explain it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. But the idea, what I said, start thinking about how to condense and harmonise. But I think there is no objection to the Borovcanin request, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that is also granted, although we don't know who the name -- I think you still need to file something, Mr. Borovcanin, even for the Registrar; and, then, perhaps you may get around the table those who would like to adduce expertise, to see whether you can bring forward one expert on the subject which will be common to all of you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you have recovered from the long journey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good. You'll be here testifying for quite some time, I suppose. Before you start your testimony, you are required to, as you know, make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Please proceed. THE WITNESS I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Manning. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Soljan, I understand, will go first for the Prosecution. She'll then be followed by the various Defence teams on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning. Before I begin, I just wanted to state that we will be primarily using Sanction for our exhibits today, due to the fact that the photographs are primarily from very large volumes and would take a very long time to show up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: My full name is Dean Paul Manning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm currently a member of the Australian Federal Police, based in Canberra, Australia. I'm employed, at the moment, at the Australian Federal Police Training College.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And how long have you been working there?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I've been a member of the Federal police since 1993, and I spent the last 18 months at the Police College following my return to Australia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe your duties and responsibilities at your current job for us?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm a senior programme facilitator on what we call "The Management of Serious Crime Programme." It's an Australian-based programme which deals with senior managers of serious crime both within Australia and internationally. The programme is considered the elite training programme for Australian managers of serious crime, and I'm responsible for running the programmes, assessing the participants, and researching the subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And where did you work prior to that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Immediately prior to resuming duties with the IFP, the Australian Federal Police, I worked with the International Inquiry Committee in relation to the All-For Food Programme which was based in New York. Immediately prior to that, I was an investigations team leader here at the ICTY involved in the investigation of Croatian offences and the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: When did you start working at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I commenced at ICTY in August of 1998. I immediately commenced duties with the Srebrenica investigations team and remained there for four years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what were the main duties and responsibilities of your work there?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It was specifically general investigative duties in support of the team investigation, but also I became the coordinator of the exhumations programme. We had a significantly large programme involved in exhumation of a number of mass graves in Bosnia, and I became the team member responsible for those exhumations and incorporating the results of those exhumations into the team's investigative work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can you explain, in a little more detail, what types of tasks did the coordinating of all of this involve?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Effectively, we monitored the ICTY exhumations team in their work. In the field, each mass grave exhumation was accompanied by a coordinator; quite often, it was myself. I would also coordinate which other investigators attended and review the reports that they had produced in relation to those exhumations. I also attended the mortuary on a very regular basis, examined the work of the mortuary, and examined the artifacts, physical exhibits, autopsy reports, and bodies that were brought to the mortuary, and I was also responsibility for returning appropriate evidentiary material to The Hague. I was also became involved at great length with the experts who were producing reports in relation to the exhumations, and ultimately assisted them in the preparation of their reports and in attending the field, and eventually in their presentation of evidence to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: When you say you assisted the experts in preparation of their reports, can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: On a number of occasions, I accompanied experts to the field to go through the various gravesites or to attend the mass grave exhumations, but also I provided them with data and information which was available at the Tribunal or the mortuary or the field. Effectively, I had an overview of all the information that we held and all the files. These exhumations had continued from 1996 until 2001, so I had an overview of the information available, the sites, the locations, and any relevant information gleaned from previous reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, what were the main objectives of the exhumations programme?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The main objectives were to locate the mass graves, exhume the graves, and to identify if the graves were related to Srebrenica, how many bodies were in the graves; then, through the aligned mortuary process, attempt to identify the individuals, identify cause of death, injuries, the gender of the individuals, and any other information that we could gain to support the investigation or guide the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us how many exhumations were carried out by the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: All the -- all the mass graves, the primary mass graves - and I can explain that term shortly - were -- there was 14 mass graves. They were all exhumed by ICTY. There was another 22 secondary mass graves which were exhumed by the ICTY, and the remaining mass graves were handed over to the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: How many exhumations have you, yourself, been present at?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I think at present, in a meaningful way, as in for some time, 11. I was present at the opening of at least eight, and I also visited other exhumations on an ad hoc basis. So I was heavily involved in at least 11 exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, let's speak generally about the process of exhumations that you participated in. Who was the personnel present at a typical exhumation?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The exhumation team consisted, in the whole or in the main, from experts from various fields. It was headed by our chief archaeologist, sometimes also an anthropologist. The team was made up of anthropologists, physical archaeologists, and other experts, including people who were able to map the grave, survey the grave. It also consisted of either former or serving police officers who acted as evidence custodians and handlers of evidence, an official photographer who photographed and videotaped the process, as well as some support staff, including backhoe and truck driver operators and technicians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And when you were in the field, what was your role during an exhumation?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Initially, much of the information concerning the location of the graves was obtained via aerial imagery, which I had access to. I would then meet with the exhumations team, and we would seek to identify where the grave was. Once we had identified the general location of the grave, it was de-mined and made secure. Normally, a trench was put through the grave or the surface of the grave was scraped off to outline the grave. The decomposition of the bodies would invariably stay in the soil, and it was quite obvious where the grave was; and then a systematic process of removing the soil and identifying and revealing the bodies would continue. The bodies would be identified via a unique number, as would any other artifacts found in the grave. That would be processed by senior crime officers, and the evidence would be secured. Eventually, the bodies would be conveyed to the mortuary facility at Visoko. When the chief archaeologist was confident that they had reached the bottom of the grave and that there were no more bodies or artifacts or body parts present, the grave would then be refilled and the area rehabilitated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Were there protocols in place when the exhumations were being done?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, a protocol was established by the -- normally the chief archaeologist. They changed over some time, but a written protocol was established. It was normally included in their report in relation to the exhumation, and it was a protocol known to the team and to the investigators. A similar protocol was established at the mortuary complex.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you illustrate, briefly, what the protocol, for example, for handling of remains was?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the protocol dealt with every step of the investigation and how evidence would be handled, including the handling of bodies. It would -- and these protocols varied slightly over the years, but it would indicate that a body would be identified within the grave; as much of the body as possible would be uncovered; photographs would be taken; various reference points taken from the body for mapping, normally consisted of all the major joints and the skull. If the body was able to be removed, if you like, in one operation, that is, it wasn't blocked by other bodies, it would be taken from the grave when it was issued a unique number, placed in a body-bag. Normally, the body itself and underneath the body was metal-detected to identify bullets or shell cases, and the details of all those processes were recorded in field notes and in photographic logs; and then the body was, as I said, stored in a refrigerated container, and periodically taken to the mortuary facility. There, their protocol indicated how they would handle the body: Record the condition of the body, photograph it; record, photograph, and examine all the clothing and artifacts from that body. It would also be forensically examined by a pathologist and/or anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And was there similar protocol for handling of evidence not directly related to the body found in the grave?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct. Physical artifacts either taken from the body or found within the grave were given a unique identifying number, photographed and recorded, handed to the scene-of-the-crime officer; and with the bodies, the artifacts and the films are treated as evidence and a chain of custody process put in place. Each of those items, including the bodies, were signed for when transported.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that the protocols varied slightly over time. Why was this?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Specifically, as the process continued, better ways of doing it, more efficient ways, or perhaps due to improvements in techniques, slight amendments would be made. If any problems were identified, that would normally be sought to be corrected in the protocol. It was also the case that there were at least three chiefs of archaeology involved, and they had slightly different processes which they would undertake. Essentially, they were the same and based on accepted standards of exhumation and examination of graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And did you ever participate in the creation or the change of any protocols?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I did, and the protocols were always discussed between myself and the chief archaeologist. In one instance, when Professor Richard Wright commenced the work of the Tribunal, I discussed with him a change to the protocol. Briefly, previously, the bodies and artifacts had been given separate numbers; that is, there is a collection of numbers for the artifacts and a separate collection of numbers for the bodies and body parts. I felt that could lead to some confusion. So following discussions with Professor Wright, he accepted that we would thereafter use one set of numbers. If a body came out of the grave first, that was number 1. If an artefact such as an identification not connected to a body came out next, that would be number 2. A slight change, but adding to the efficiency of the system. And those sorts of changes were made on occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, with regard to evidence selection, what was the process of getting evidence from the grave moved to whatever the next step was supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Following the protocols, effectively anything that was found within the grave was examined by the chief archaeologist. If it was something that should be collected, such as, you know, shell cases or bullets or artifacts, identifications, they were automatically collected. On occasion, pieces of what could be described as rubbish, car parts, pieces of branch were located, and, initially, they were treated as evidence. They were examined, photographed, and seized, and handled by the senior crime officers. On occasion, they became quite important as pieces of evidence. In one particular grave, the type of rocks became important, as they could be matched to another grave. And in one grave, rocks which had been basically stone tools were found within the grave, and they were later found in -- very similar stones were found in another grave, leading to a connection. So on occasion, artifacts such as stones were considered important. But, in any event, artifacts were seized, a photograph process recorded, treated as evidence, conveyed to the mortuary where they were signed for, secured, and examined.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Were these artifacts retained by the mortuary? What happens with the artifacts once they were at the mortuary?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the artifacts were conveyed to the mortuary, where they were also secured. Because in the field it's difficult to examine artifacts in detail, that examination was conducted by the mortuary. So they would be cleaned, photographed, details recorded, and then they would be stored. The normal process would be, at either periods during the year or at the end of the year, I would go through all the artifacts, physically examine all the artifacts, examine the photographs and records of those items, and make a selection as to what would be conveyed to The Hague. Generally, blindfolds and ligatures were certainly conveyed to The Hague, shell cases. Some of the artifacts would be personal effects such as plastic combs or cigarette lighters. Those items were not conveyed to The Hague. Clothing was not conveyed. And whilst a number of identification documents were returned to The Hague, we took the view that they should remain within Bosnia and be handed over to the Bosnian authorities to assist in identification processes. So I would also take a representative sample of identification, and then I would rely on the photographs and records of those items. I would, on occasion, consult the team if there were items that would potentially be of use, and I would then either transport those items myself or they would be shipped safe-hand to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, did you ever participate in any collections of surface remains?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No, I did not; although, on occasion, surface remains were located as we started the exhumation process. So there was surface remains connected to the mass grave, but I and the ICTY team did not collect general surface remains. We concentrated on mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And how long was the ICTY responsible for the exhumation of Srebrenica-related mass graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The first Srebrenica exhumations started in 1996, and they continued until 2001. At that time, the responsibility for exhuming the remaining secondary graves was handed to the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, assisted by ICMP, the International Commission for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Did you participate in that hand-over process?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could you please make pauses between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you both hear that? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies. Yes, I was particularly involved in that process. I had been responsible for drafting the memorandum of understanding, and in very lengthy and detailed discussions with the Bosnian authorities and with the ICTY management as to how we would hand over those graves. Also, at that time, we had created a small ICTY team to monitor the exhumations conducted by the Bosnians, and I was responsible for organising that team and supporting that team in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Do you know how many graves were handed over to the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I think it was 20 graves, in the area of 20 graves. It was all the known secondary graves that we had at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And since the hand-over, have you ever monitored any of the Bosnian exhumations of graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. We had the ICTY monitoring team in place, and I visited on a very regular basis, but I was also present for several weeks at the exhumation of Ravnice 2, which was conducted by the Bosnian Commission and

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I was also present for several days at another exhumation. I think it was Cancari Road 11; and then, on occasion, whilst I was in Bosnia, I would visit the ongoing exhumations.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And based on your observations, would you say that the mandate or the process used by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons is similar as the mandate or the process used by the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Much of the process was similar, and ICMP would staff their team with archaeologists and anthropologists, but the ICTY team and the ICTY process was forensically driven to collect evidence for support, to support the trials. Our focus was predominately on gathering evidence. The Bosnian Commission is much more focused on recovering bodies. They attempt, in a very dedicated fashion, to try and recover evidence. However, their primary motive for the exhumations is to remove the bodies, have them examined and identified, and have the remains returned to the family and loved ones. So their process is much more driven by removing the bodies from the graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And have there been any more recent findings of the graves, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of a number of graves that have been located by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons. I discussed those -- some of those graves on a mission to Bosnia in 2005. I also went to a number of those sites in 2005, and I've since reviewed records and photographs held or produced by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, which detailed the new mass graves located. I believe it's five or six new graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher, please, to place on e-court Exhibit P03008, and if we could move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, have you seen this photograph before?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And can you please explain what it is?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I recognise the photo to be, in my opinion, a mass grave. It's clear that the mess in the middle of it is human bodies, and I believe the edges in that photograph would be the edges of the grave. Effectively, it's something that I recognise as very similar to the mass graves that I've seen.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Do you know where this photo is from or who it was obtained from?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The photo was obtained from the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Okay. But you, yourself, have not been at this location?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Not at this location; although, as I said, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Microphone not activated] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm trying to oblige. Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going to object to this. This is obviously something that has not been dealt with before in this courtroom, nor will it be dealt with afterwards. Furthermore, this witness doesn't even know the location of this grave, even though he may have seen a picture of it after his employment terminated with the Office of the Prosecutor. I think this is the first instance of which may be many where he's going past your ruling on his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. Ms. Soljan, what's your response to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this photo, the photos obtained by the ICMP, are simply being shown to him, not for the truth, but simply to demonstrate that he has reviewed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to be what she said in her question, number 1, and they're not being shown for the truth of the matter. I submit they are just being shown to inflame Your Honours, as professional jurors, even though professional you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were on the right track until now, Mr. Meek. That kind of language or statements, you shouldn't be making. Sorry, Mr. Zivanovic, I apologise to you. I didn't see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just said that the witness was called to give his opinion about these photos. It is said at the page 23 -- 24, excuse me, line 20. He is called to give his opinion about his -- these photos, and he gave his opinion, what he believes that these photos depicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, could you give me the exhibit number again?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: The exhibit number, Your Honour, is P03008, and it's the second page, so it's X020-3642.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So let's start from the tail-end part of Mr. Meek's submission. Mr. Meek, we don't -- we hope we'll never hear again submissions to the effect that being shown photos like this is intended or would ultimately have the effect and that's why they are intended to be inflammatory. Do you know how many dead people I have seen in my life, and my colleagues, and postmortems I have assisted in my life, so come on. That's number 1. As for the rest, you are right. Mr. Manning has already stated that he has been on-site where there were mass graves and other gravesites being exhumed. I think you have every right to show him and refer him to those, but I don't think you need to refer to his testimony by means of reference to photos of other gravesites he hasn't been to and which he cannot testify upon except by looking, I mean. So let's proceed with your next question, and you are, of course, by all means authorised to show him anything else with which he is familiar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, are you -- are you aware of any new surface remains findings in recent times?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I was aware from an examination of the ICMP data and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise. I hate to stop this testimony, but it's the same objection. He's aware after the fact of the ICMP findings which are -- have never been before this Chamber, and I honestly submit they won't be from looking at the OTP's calender of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an integral part of his testimony. If anything, he's summarising evidence that he has reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he's also already been asked about surface remains and whether he's seen any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree, he was asked about the surface remains, and perhaps objections should have been made; however, he said he didn't -- had nothing to do with the surface remains. There was a negative answer to that question, that he did not participate in the collection of surface remains. While it may be a large body of their evidence, we know that, and that's why I believe Your Honour has correctly ruled that anything knew and anything from the ICMP or the BCMP is new. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Soljan, do you wish to add any remain?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: No. Only to remark that this is not how I understood your ruling. I understood your ruling to be only in respect to experts that were not in evidence. That did not cover ICMP, ICMP not being an expert, as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As for the ICMP, anyway. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just to make things clear, our concern that we expressed earlier on, when we handed our decision, was to make sure that this witness is not used to introduce in the records expertise of others which is not in the record and which has-- will not be introduced. What the question by Ms. Soljan to Mr. Manning amounts to has got nothing to do with expertise. It was a very simple question, which refers to a fact: "Are you aware, Mr. Manning, of any surface remains findings in recent times?" And he is either away or he's not aware. He says, "I was aware," and he was explaining to us how he became aware of this, I suppose. So he should be allowed to continue finishing that; and, then, if there are further objections as we go along, we'll entertain them and decide them appropriately. Yes, Ms. Soljan. Actually, I think you should repeat the question, which I have repeated, so he can -- Mr. Manning, you can take it up from where you left it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of the collection of surface remains, specifically from examining ICMP data; but also in my 2005 mission, I attended the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish, because we still haven't gotten to expertise, Mr. Meek. Please, sit down and let him finish. Go ahead, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I specifically examined or sought to examine the collection of surface remains with the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons and the ICMP. I visited with Mr. Morat Hutic [phoen], who is based in Tuzla, and we went through his records, various maps, and identified areas that surface remains had been collected from. He provided me with codes in relation to the designation of those collections. I reviewed Tuzla Cantonal Court files in relation to the collection of those surface remains, including the designations of those areas, including some photographs. I also attended the area of some of the mass graves sites identified by the Bosnian Commission, as well as some of the collection areas. I must say, however, the collection areas were of a very wide area, and many of them were in areas which would be considered. Unsafe, so I generally viewed areas where I had been advised surface remains had been collected from. And as I say, the ICMP data contained codes which I was able to recognise as collections of surface remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Meek, did you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. There was a comment earlier that the ICMP is not an expert. It's an organisation that is full of experts, and one of the names he just mentioned is an expert, I believe, pathologist. This is the information that we believe that you have said is not admissible because it's new. It has never been presented in this courtroom, nor will it be, nor will there be any experts, pathologists, forensic anthropologists, coming from the ICMP or the BCMP. These are organizations full of experts, Your Honour, and they're just trying to boot-strap this in, even with your ruling, and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Manning's testimony in relation to ICMP data has nothing to do with underlying expertise, with DNA analysis, pathology reports, et cetera. All he's doing is summarising the numbers through his knowledge of site names, as he's mentioned already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just briefly in response, Your Honours, when he's talking about surface remains, there has to be an expert, a geologist involved in that. So it's just not fair, what they're trying to say, that this has nothing to do with any expertise through either one of these organisations, because they're full of experts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question, Mr. Meek. Don't you think that what the witness has testified, really, is that in relation to his knowledge and exploration of surface remains, he used various sources, and these are the sources that he used?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Without introducing into evidence these sources, because he is not, at least until now, he is not introducing into evidence these sources. He's just stated -- he's just stating how he came to know about these surface remains and from where and from whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm, again, trying to answer your question, Your Honour. I don't believe the witness has testified that he has any type of expertise in surface remains, or exploration of surface remains, since he testified earlier that he had nothing to do with the surface remains or collection of the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I never mentioned that he is giving us expertise on these surface remains. Anyway, let me consult with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have a question to Ms. Soljan. Ms. Soljan, you said that he's going to -- he is summarising the numbers. What numbers do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The number of dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Number of dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In order to reach a certain number, do you not need expertise, in light of the number of bones, number of artifacts, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Well, as his testimony will show, the analysis that he carried out, the review of the data that he carried out, did not -- well, he will testify about the lack of it or that there was no need of expertise for this. Basically, it was his prior knowledge of the exhumations process carried out by the ICTY and analysis of ICMP data. Very simple, ICMP data. We're not talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so far we can proceed with this question and the related line of questions, and then we'll see how it progresses and decide accordingly. But there is nothing irregular so far or in conflict with our previous decision. So, yes, Ms. Soljan, he's given us all his sources of information and what he started doing after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, have you recently reviewed any materials concerning numbers of surface remains?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, I reviewed the files which had been produced by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, and the ICMP data contains records of missing persons -- sorry, surface remains.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could the usher place Exhibit P03007 into e-court. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen that document before.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No objection. Is there an English translation of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't ask me. I don't know. Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: No, there isn't, Your Honour. It's just a one-page short summary, but we can provide a translation during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Would you be happy with that, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is, Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Given that it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness answers this question, we'd like to know whether the witness speaks B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Do you speak the Serbo-Croat language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not, Your Honour, and I don't read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take it, then, you did not prepare this document yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it was shown to me and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And explained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and explained to me in English, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think if someone needs -- if someone reads out the words in that language, we can have them simultaneously translated. Ms. Soljan, you certainly know the language, so you can read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: It says: [B/C/S spoken] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we didn't get the translation. That was the whole idea.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "The table overview of bodies exhumed collected on surface by years. Exhumations and the victims pertain to 1995 only." This is the understanding of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not since 1995? In other words, I'm asking this question. I don't understand the language, so I find it's strange if it's for 1995 only, and then you have a list going to each year after that until 2007.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's very abbreviated. What it says is the victims are from 1995, or what it is meant to convey. It has columns which say "Year of exhumation"; a second column which says "The number of gathered cases from the surface"; and the last column which says "The number of identified who have been gathered from the surface."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Might we have an indication of where this document originated?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, do you know where this document is from?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I understand it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you answer, yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not really concerned about this testimony, but I find it quite difficult to know how this witness, who doesn't read the Serbo-Croat language and who doesn't write it, can comment on this document and can tell us where it comes from; whereas, he can't even read the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think the two segments are mutually exclusively. I mean, he could know the origin of this document, even though he didn't produce it himself and he doesn't read the language, if someone has shown it to him and told him this has been prepared by -- or "This has been prepared by myself; I'm going to translate it to you." So, yes, let's proceed. Mr. Manning, who showed you this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this particular document was shown to me by Ms. Soljan; however, I can indicate that I've seen a similar versions of this document in records held at the Tuzla Cantonal Court. I can't say and I don't believe it's the same document, but the same format. And whilst I don't read Bosnian/Serbo/Croat, I'm familiar with enough of the language to know that "godina" is year and "exhumatia" is exhumation. I can make out some of those details. I have seen the precursor to this document in the Tuzla Cantonal Court records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Soljan. You still don't know who, in other words, is the origin or the source of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The origin of this particular document I believe to be from the Bosnian authorities. It was contained in a file that I was told was produced by the Bosnian authorities. The previous version I had seen was produced by the Tuzla Cantonal Court and the investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So, again, all we know from this witness, it was shown by the Prosecutor to him, The question of who generated it, other than the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, is very broad, and my specific question is: What -- which expert in that organisation did this, or which person, and what profession were they in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You can deal with that on cross-examination, Mr. Meek. Let's proceed. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If I could just try to help briefly. As you know, exhumations are ongoing. They're happening today. Mr. Manning, in his 2005 contract, went around and learned as much as he could from the authorities. He has -- we have additional information that he has reviewed. This last document, for example, it's a hearsay document. But if we're to keep up with the exhumations to any degree so that you can see what's coming out of these graves and on the surfaces, we need to rely on people like Mr. Manning and his expertise to provide you with the hearsay that's out there. Otherwise, we would be bringing numerous experts, which really aren't necessary. This is picking up bones from the ground. This is pulling out bones from -- it's just a very big crime scene. So getting involved in expertise, yes, there are -- the identifications are made by DNA, and that is an expertise. That was the same kind of DNA work that Mr. Helge Brunborg relied on, which went in unobjected. So we can come in and bring in the DNA experts, if you want to see that. But what Mr. Manning is doing is fundamentally what he did in 2005, in trying to get for you the best summary of the graves and the bodies and the people. That's all this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. At the very outset of his testimony, the witness stated that he had been engaged primarily in the collection of evidence for the purposes of the criminal proceedings and for the purposes of this Tribunal, and he said that once the authority for the conducting of the exhumations had been handed to the local authorities from the Tribunal, the local authorities primarily focused on the collection of evidence for the purposes of identification in order for the families to learn the fate of their missing family members. Therefore, the witness has here been telling us about a document which he says he doesn't know but believes to have been issued by the Bosnian authorities, and says that he saw a similar document to this one during his mission in Tuzla. He was in Tuzla, as he himself told us, in 2005. In this document, we have data from 2007. We also know that in the meantime, there were recent identification processes, and the information he is giving us cannot correspond to the information we see in the document here today. Therefore, the witness should clearly tell us when and on what occasion he saw the document, and whether he was told from whom the document was obtained, and he should tell us, if in any way, he participated in the drafting of the data we see contained in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to do any of this, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Meek. I think things have been clear. He has not had anything to do with the compilation of this document. He's never pretended that this is the same document he saw in Tuzla, but that it is on a similar concept or on a similar structure, that it was shown to him by Ms. Soljan, and that he believes that this came from the Bosnian authorities. So let's move with your next question, please. I didn't realise it's time for the break. I think you either wait and we will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, do you still wish to address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I would just like to respond to the last submission of Mr. McCloskey regarding Mr. Brunborg's testimony. Actually, he said that the part of Mr. Brunborg's testimony related to DNA analysis was not objected, but I just recall that all testimony of Mr. Brunborg, including his report, was contested, including the DNA findings or DNA mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, Mr. Zivanovic. Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, in the course of your investigations, did you identify mass graves related to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I was present at the location or identification of a number of mass graves, and I was present when those mass graves were defined and the start of the exhumation process. I think I was present when we found the exact location of eight mass graves, and I personally was involved in the location of three additional mass graves predominantly using aerial imagery.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll go into that shortly. But before we do, what do you mean by "mass grave"?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, speaking as a layman, and I know the term is defined by archaeologists, effectively a grave, a place where individuals are buried, the normal definition is -- would contain at least two individuals, the remains of two individuals. We've taken the view, within the exhumations project, that it would generally mean a great deal more than that. The majority of the graves that we have exhumed have contained multiple bodies. I think the smallest was three, the next was nine, then 33, then into the hundreds.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And what types of mass graves have you seen?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, we had defined two types of mass grave: A primary mass grave and a secondary mass grave. And if I can explain, simply, the primary mass grave is a grave where individuals were first placed following their death, their execution. On many occasions, they were executed at the gravesite and then their grave was sealed. At some stage in the future, those graves were opened, were disturbed, the contents robbed or parts of the contents robbed from the grave and placed into another grave, and that grave or that type of grave would be a secondary grave; that is, a grave where the bodies were placed a second time. I'm also aware or believe that there is a tertiary grave which, by simple definition, bodies were removed from a secondary grave and placed into an unknown grave, which would be a third-level grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could I please get on Sanction Exhibit P01899.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, can you comment on what this picture represents?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm quite familiar with this image. It's a photograph of the Kozluk mass grave which was exhumed by the ICTY. Effectively, it shows a number of things. Clearly, there are bodies on the surface. I'm aware that the posture of those bodies -- of some of those bodies indicate that their wrists were bound. It's clearly evident that their wrists were tied, and I have examined the ligatures and autopsy reports relating to those bodies. If you like, the bodies are laying on the surface of the soil as it would have been when they were first killed and placed in the grave, and then they were covered with soil. That soil's been removed to expose that photograph that you see. If you look to the bottom right of that photograph, you see a trench dug through the normal or previous surface of the grave. That trench appears to have been dug by a machine, as there are machine teeth marks in the wall of the grave, they're evident, and what that shows is that at some stage that area has been removed from the grave. So, effectively, some process has come along which has removed part of the bodies from that grave after they were initially buried. To us, that's an indication that that grave was robbed. The term means that the contents were taken from the grave. You can see that some of the bodies in that image have been bisected, have been cut, and parts of those bodies have been removed.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to this picture, what would -- what would a secondary mass grave that you have seen look like, in terms of positioning of bodies?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In this image, you can see the bodies mostly fully articulated, in that they are all together. It's clear that they are -- have fallen down or are laying down, and you can discern the individual bodies. Generally, in a secondary grave, you will see that the bodies are jumbled up. They have been placed there predominantly by machine, and that has meant that the bodies have tumbled together, many body parts, and that many of the bodies have been broken up. Generally, a secondary grave will show a great deal of disturbance of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how did you go about identifying mass graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Predominantly, either witness or survivor accounts we used, and I must caution that I wasn't at the Tribunal in 1996 or 1997 when a number of the graves were located. But without testimony or witness or survivor account, we relied heavily on aerial imagery provided by the US government. We would look at that imagery, attend the corresponding area of Bosnia, and examine the area with an archaeologist, attempting to locate the grave and hopefully locate the remains of at least two individuals to show that it was a mass grave.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And, specifically, what kind of information did aerial imagery provide you with?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The images normally contained a date and an approximate time, as well as a label, normally a location. We would know from that the general area. We would compare that to a map. On some of the aerial imagery, you also had some indications placed there by the provider, but generally you had a roadway or a location, a disturbed piece of earth which was clearly visible, and a heading on the photo as to where the general location was.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And did aerial imagery alone allow you to identify the graves as Srebrenica graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The imagery did not, specifically; however, it did provide a date range for when the graves were created. Effectively, those images showed that they were created at or around the time of the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I could have on Sanction Exhibit P01760.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is, Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a section of a map. It shows the area of the Kozluk primary mass grave. In fact, with the assistance of OTP staff, I had placed that circle around the Kozluk grave in previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could we go on to the next exhibit, P01761, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you describe what this image represents?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a -- one of the aerial imagery which was provided to us. It's a two-pane image. It shows, on the left, the Drina River to the left and top of the image, and a date, the 5th of July. It shows an area in Kozluk which I'm familiar with, and you can see the roadway and certain features. On the image on the 17th of July, on the right-hand pane, you see that same area and some very obvious signs of physical disturbance of the soil and what I believe to be, or know to be from the location, a trench and various disturbance of the soil.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could we go to the next image, please, Exhibit P01763.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: What does this image demonstrate?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is again a split pane, a two-pane view. On the left is a 7th of September image showing those areas of disturbance; and on the 27th of September, you see a further disturbance of that area. In effect, the previous areas have been significantly increased and disturbed.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And what is the significance of that image?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That image shows the opening of the primary mass grave at Kozluk and the -- effectively, the removal of the bodies -- some of the bodies from those graves. You can see clearly on that image track marks from vehicles, where heavy machinery has moved the earth and created a disturbance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on to Exhibit P01797, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you describe what this represents, please?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is again --

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: You can comment on that as well. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, this is a location map. It shows the mass grave, the primary disturbed mass grave at the place called Petkovci Dam. It was referred to by various names, but the Dam at Petkovci or Petkovci Dam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can I could have the next photograph. That would be P01746, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you comment on this picture, please?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is again a split-image view from aerial imagery. On the left is a shot from the 5th of July, 1995. It shows the earthen wall of the dam. If you look to the left of the image, the water would be to the left of that image, and you can see various access roadways.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And the next image, P01747.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 65 ter number of the map, Ms. Soljan?.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Oh, it's P01744.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the right-hand pane shows exactly the same area, and you can see on that it's the 27th of July. You can see a disturbance in the soil, in the rock fill of the dam wall. The markings on that image were placed there by the provider. Effectively, what that shows is the creation of the Petkovci Dam mass grave, in the earthen of the dam, and that was the area that was later exhumed by the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next image, which is P01747.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you comment on that, Mr. Manning, please?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This again shows the two views. Again, the water is on the left of the photo, and it's the disturbance of that grave, that mass grave, between the 7th of September and the 27th of September, 1995. Whilst the image is perhaps difficult to see, in the original it's clearly evident that that area of disturbance has been dug up, re-disturbed, and the soil placed back on top of the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And the significance of that is?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: On exhumation by ICTY, the mass grave at the dam was found to contain very few human remains, very many small parts of human remains. This image and the resultant exhumation shows that the bodies contained in this mass grave were removed and taken to another or other sites.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can we now go to Exhibit P01797, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is, Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is another location map. It shows the area of the Branjevo military farm. The Drina River is on the right, and the Kozluk mass grave would be below these images -- this image.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And the next image, P01799.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This image is familiar to me. It is the Branjevo military farm. It shows, amongst other things, the mass grave which was created at that site. It shows a great deal of vehicle tracks. It shows some of the locations of buildings, the places where pigs -- a pig farm, and it shows what I believe to be bodies in the middle of the left of the image.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Are you familiar with who made the markings in yellow on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The markings were produced, as I recall, by the former Srebrenica team leader, Jean-Rene Ruez, and placed on the image. I must also point out I've been to that location on a number of occasions and am familiar with those buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can we go to Exhibit P01723 -- my apologies, Exhibit P01800.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you comment on what this image represents?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This shows, effectively, the same area with the pigsty on the -- sorry, the pig farm on the right of the image, where that road comes down, and it shows the mass gravesite. This photograph, along with others, indicate the disturbance of that primary mass grave, which was again opened up and a significant number of the bodies and remains were removed from that grave, and then the grave was re-sealed. You can also see various vehicle tracks in that image.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you indicate for the Trial Chamber when this image is dated?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This image is dated 21 September 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: What is the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That is the date range, if you like, when many of the primary mass graves were opened; when many of the secondary mass graves were created; and over the next several weeks, the primary graves were robbed of their contents, placed into the secondary graves; and then both sets of graves were sealed until ICTY or ICMP and the Bosnians opened them up again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And Exhibit P01801.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you see in this image?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This image is dated the 27th of September, 1995. It shows exactly the same area of the Branjevo military farm. I indicate that the small box and comments are provided, placed on the image by the provider, but shows the primary mass grave in the process of being opened and robbed and sealed. It's part of that process that occurred over several weeks in September and October of 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: If we could now go to Exhibit P01719, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is, please?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is another location map of the mass grave at Orahovac. You can see that the Dam at Petkovci is at the top middle of that image. The Orahovac grave, there's two mass graves there, primarily disturbed mass graves, and it was also referred to as "Lazete," so it has two names, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. The next Exhibit is P01721.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this image shows?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is another split-pane view of the Orahovac 1 and 2 mass graves. The first pane on the left is 5 July 1995. The top line in the image is a road. The line in the middle, the straight line in the middle is, a railway track. You can see that there is no significant disturbance in the area. On the 27th of July, 1995, in the other pane, you can see two areas of disturbance; one near the roadway and one on the other side of the railway line. They are the mass graves of Orahovac 1, near the roadway; and Orahovac 2, near the railway line. I was present for the exhumation of both of those graves, certainly the second half of Orahovac 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have the next exhibit, P01723, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you comment on this, Mr. Manning, please?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This image shows the Orahovac-Lazete 1 mass grave. The image on the left is taken on the 7th of September, 1995. It shows the original primary mass grave. And on the image on the right, taken on the 27th of September, 1995, it shows the clear disturbance of that site. This series of photographs show that grave being opened and robbed and eventually closed.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And the next exhibit, P01724.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the corresponding grave on the railway line, Lazete-Orahovac 2, taken on the same day; and it shows again the 7th of September, the original disturbed area, which is a primary mass grave; and then the disturbance and robbery process of that grave around the time of the 27th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can we go to Exhibit P01648, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is, Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a location map showing the Zeleni Jadar secondary mass graves. These are all secondary mass graves. They're south of the city of Srebrenica, and it shows the graves spread across various roadways. Again, this image was created by myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And Exhibit P01649.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you comment on this, please?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a compilation of two aerial imagery. It shows the Zeleni Jadar graves 1 through to 6. I, with the assistance of others, created this image. I would point out that at Zeleni Jadar 1 is, in fact, two graves, and that should be Zeleni Jadar 1A and Zeleni Jadar 1B.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And going on to P01650.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, this is a split image. It, in fact, shows Zeleni Jadar 1, which we knew about early on; and then Zeleni Jadar 2 is also -- sorry, 1B is also visible, which we discovered or probed at a later date. But effectively, again, it shows the 7th of September, 1995, no disturbance; on at least the 2nd of October, 1995, a disturbance which has created a mass grave, a secondary mass grave.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And Exhibit P01651, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: What does this represent?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is another split aerial image. On the left, you have the two graves created at least on the 18th of October or roundabout. On the right-hand pane, on the 20th of October, you can see a disturbance, a further disturbance of those two graves, indicating that those graves have been filled in. I was present when Zeleni Jadar 1B was located, and we located the remains of multiple human beings within that secondary mass grave.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can we go on to Exhibit P01652.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you please describe this image?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is another split image. The original is clearer; but in the middle of the image, you have the roadway.
