To the bottom right -- sorry, to the bottom of both images, you have the Zeleni Jadar River. On the 24th of August, 1995 pane, you can see the areas not disturbed; and on the 2nd of October, 1995 pane, you can see clearly a disturbance and a large trench is visible, and that's the Zeleni Jadar 2 secondary mass grave.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And for the record, could you just indicate where the Zeleni Jadar 2 disturbance can be seen?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: On the right-hand pane, you can see the -- perhaps in the middle right of that image, and it's labelled by the yellow marker "ZJ-2".

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could I have the next exhibit, P01653.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And, again, can you describe what you see on this image?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Another split image. On the left is the same view, Zeleni Jadar Road and River. It's taken on the 20th of October, 1995, and shows the Zeleni Jadar secondary grave. On the pane on the 23rd of October, 1995, you can clearly see evidence that that has been disturbed and the grave has been sealed up sometime between the 20th of October and the 23rd of October. And, again, the grave is marked by a yellow arrow and "ZJ-2".

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: The next exhibit is P01654.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you please describe this image?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, a split image, and it shows the next grave in the Zeleni Jadar series. On the 7th of September, 1995, there's no disturbance visible. On the 2nd of October, 1995, you can clearly see an area of a mass grave which has been created, and it's marked "ZJ-3".

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: The next image, P01655.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you comment on this one, please?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a single image. It shows the same area on the bow of that road where the Zeleni Jadar 3 mass grave is located. So on the 20th of October, 1995, that area had again been disturbed and sealed up. In effect, the mass grave was closed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And Exhibit P01656.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This image is a split pane but it's a little bit different, in that they are on top of each other. The top pane, marked "7th of September, 1995," shows the Zeleni Jadar roadway. Clearly, there is no disturbance in that area. On the bottom image, on the 12th of October, 1995, you can see two areas of disturbance marked as "ZJ-4" and" ZJ-5". The ZJ-5 grave, or Zeleni Jadar 5 grave, I was present when that was open in 1998 and present for some of the exhumation of that grave.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Exhibit P01657, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This single image, taken on the 18th of October, 1995, shows those two graves, those two secondary graves which have been sealed, and those images are marked "ZJ-4" and" ZJ-5".

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And Exhibit P01658.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is again a split image. On the 7th of September, 1995, no disturbances visible; and, in fact, on the original, it's clearer. On the 27th of September, 1995, on the right-hand pane, you can see a clear trench has been excavated, and it's marked as "ZJ-6". I was present to identify and locate that grave and present when it was opened and during parts of the exhumation of that grave.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And Exhibit P01659.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, the same area in a split pane. The 12th of October, on the left, shows the trench clearly visible; and on the right, on the 18th of October, 1995, clearly that trench has been filled in, and you can see vehicle marks and features. I was able to view many of those features when we examined the grave prior to opening it.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Manning, during the course of your work at the ICTY, did you actually have a chance to review all of the aerial images and topographic marks that are in the exhibit list, including the graves of Cerska, Cancari, Hodzici, and Liplje?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I'm very familiar with those aerial imagery and maps and other charts related to those graves; and, in fact, I produced many of the markings on those items.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: What type of information were you able to glean from the aerial imagery concerning the graves, in summary?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Effectively, we were provided with the date and sometimes the approximate time that those images were taken. We're able to see the clear disturbance, see where it was located, use that as an aid in locating the actual grave. We're also able to see, in many instances, a similarity in construction of those graves prior to them being filled in, and it also provided location of other features, which helped us identify where the graves were.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the interests of saving time, unless you prefer otherwise, I do not propose to actually show the remaining aerials and topographic maps that are listed on the exhibit list, but I will be seeking to tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any of the Defence teams wish to comment on that? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Proceed as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Then, for the record, the exhibits -- these exhibits are exhibits related to the Glogova 1 and 2 dossier, which are Exhibit numbers P01605 and P01608 to 1611; the ones relating to primary graves Cerska, P01640 and 1642; relating to secondary graves of Cancari, P01842 to 1869; Hodzici, P01821 to 1832, as well as 2168; and, finally, P01833 to 1840 for the Liplje dossier.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Now, let's turn briefly to the map that you have at hand --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Not an objection, but she was speaking kind of quickly and there's at least five different sites that did not show up on the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That can be remedied later, provided -- the important this is that you are aware which ones he was talking about. If you have any doubts, Mr. Meek, we can ask Ms. Soljan to repeat the names, at least, without the need to refer to the exhibit number. We have Glogova, we have Cerska, Cancari, Liplje --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And Hodzici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and Hodzici. So there is only one missing. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Let's turn briefly to the map, which is to Exhibit P02996.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you tell us who created this?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This map in this form was created by the OTP. It's based almost completely on a very similar map that I produced for previous trials. I, with the assistance of other OTP staff, produced the base maps, then added the markings and the symbols; and on this map, there are additional graves identified from -- since my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please describe what this map represents?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, it effectively shows the area where the mass graves have been located. It shows the north and the south, and it lists every primary mass grave that we're aware of and every secondary mass grave. It labels those graves, primary mass graves, in red. It also shows execution points of Pilica Dom and Branjevo military -- sorry, and Kravica warehouse. It also shows the red lines which link some of the primary and secondary graves, and the reason we link those graves are in text within that arrow. And on the southern side, the southern end of the map, in a similar manner, it identifies primary mass graves, secondary mass graves, and the links between those graves. It also shows the -- some graves which were identified by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons and ICMP.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you, for the Trial Chamber, indicate the name for the primary graves that are on this map?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: On the northern edge of -- end of the map, you have the primary mass grave of Branjevo military farm disturbed; Kozluk, which is disturbed; the dam near Petkovci, which was also disturbed; Orahovac 1 and 2, also known as Lazete 1 and 2, which were also disturbed. That's to the north of the map. The southern part of the map, you have the understood sites at Cerska, Konjevic Polje 1, Konjevic Polje 2, Nova Kasaba 1999, Nova Kasaba 1996, Ravnice 1 and 2, and Glogova 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What about Sandici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Sandici is a grave identified by the Bosnian Commission, and I have been to that location but wasn't present or involved in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I asked because you left it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And of the primary graves in the southern location, are any of them disturbed?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'd indicated the undisturbed graves. The disturbs graves are Glogova 1 and 2. The rest of the graves, including Ravnice, Konjevic Polje 1 and 2, Cerska, and Nova Kasaba, both Nova Kasabas, are undisturbed primary mass graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you also name all the secondary mass graves or mass grave clusters and connect them to the mass graves you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: If you look at the northern top-most part of the map, you have a collection of secondary mass graves on the Hodzici Road. They are 1 through 7. Three of those graves connected directly to Orahovac 1 and 2. You also have a collection of graves along the Liplje road, Liplje road. Those graves, initially, were Liplje 1 to 4, and Liplje 7 has since been located by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons. I indicate that I had visited that site prior to its exhumation with Mr. Murat Hutic. Those graves were connected or -- sorry, Liplje 2 was connected to the primary grave at the dam near Petkovci. You also have a considerable number of graves along the Cancari Road, 1 through 13. Some of those graves on the eastern side are connected to the Kozluk primary mass grave; that is, Cancari 3 and Cancari 2. And on the other end of the Cancari secondary mass graves, we have a connection from the Branjevo military farm to Cancari Road 12. On the southern part of that map, you have a connection from the execution point at Kravica warehouse to the primary undisturbed mass grave at Ravnice 1 and 2, and you also have a connection to the disturbed primary graves of Glogova 1 and 2. Down at the bottom of the map is the Zeleni Jadar mass graves, 1A, 1B through to 6. They're secondary graves. We have a connection from the Glogova mass graves to Zeleni Jadar 5 and 6. Also shown on that image are graves identified by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, Bljeceva 1 and 2 and 3, and Budak, as well as the mass grave of Sandici. I have visited Bljeceva 1 and 2 and Budak 1.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now could I please have Exhibit P00649 on Sanction, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is, please?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a topographic map produced by, I believe, commercial satellite imagery. It shows the area in the south of the map behind me, and it includes or travelled from the Kravica warehouse to the left of that image, to Ravnice 1 and 2 mass gravesite, down to Glogova 1 and 2 in the middle right of that image. I'd indicate that the distance between Kravica warehouse and Glogova 1 and 2 is approximately eight kilometres. It also shows, in the insert at the top left, the Sandici mass grave identified by the Bosnians; but also in that image, there's a white spot which is the Sandici meadow, where individuals were collected prior to execution at the Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can I now have -- for the record, this was actually Exhibit P02996, and the next exhibit I'd like to see is P00649. Apologies. For the record, that was P02995, and the next exhibit will be P00649.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you comment on this, please, Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a chart which I produced and presented in previous testimony. It lists, at the top of the image, primary mass graves. You'll see that at least Ravnice 1 and 2 were not included, as they weren't known at that time. Along the bottom of the image are some secondary mass graves. The lines on that image indicate where there are links between the primary graves at the top and the secondary graves at the bottom, and they list those -- the reasons why we know that those graves are linked.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And although we'll go into more detail about that shortly, can you just list the reasons?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Basically, we were able to link the graves via shell case examination; from soil and pollen samples; from the examination of cloth, blindfolds, and ligatures; and also from artifacts such as bottle labels and broken green glass or parts of building material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The exhibit number for this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is P00649.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page number?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: The page number is 14 -- sorry, 15. The ERN is 0095-0927.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check it out later on?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Will do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, in your experience as investigator on multiple mass gravesites, was it possible to determine whether the executions had taken place at the gravesites, themselves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, at many of the sites, we had -- or some of the sites, we had survivor testimony, and I'm sure the Chamber has heard testimony from other individuals. But also we were able to see that clearly individuals had been shot in the location of the mass grave. It was possible to see that from the position the bodies had fallen or were laying. Some individuals had fallen forward. Some individuals had a posture which indicated that they had fallen. And during the examination, we would examine the body. You would see injuries to the body, or to the clothing, consistent, to my view, with injuries; and then you would examine underneath the body and often locate bullets in the soil or in other bodies corresponding to those injuries. That, to me and to the experts in their reports, indicated that those individuals had been killed in situ, in place. It is also instances where it was clear that individuals had been shot and had crawled or moved away, and there is a specific instance at the Kozluk grave where that is evident.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit P020 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry to interject. The witness has already testified in the past five minutes or so that several of these gravesites were done by the BCMP, not the ICTY; and now he just testified about the experts and their reports. Now, if any of these experts and their reports have not been before this Trial Chamber or are not coming before this Trial Chamber, I think that evidence is, under your ruling, inadmissible; and, perhaps, he could point out if any of these experts that he just referred to were experts from the ICMP or the BCMP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't said that they were from those sources. Yes, Ms. Soljan, would you like to comment on the objection --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- or ask questions to the witness straightaway?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I can ask questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, who made the observations regarding the killings in situ?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was referring specifically to Dr. William Hagland in his exhumations of the 1996 exhumations; Dr. Richard Wright in his later examinations from 1998 onwards; Mr. Jose Pablo Baraybar from the ICTY; and I believe, from recollection, Mr. Freddie Pecurelli [phoen], also from the ICTY. I was not referring to experts from any other organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can we go to the next exhibit on Sanction, which is P02063-149.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, can you comment on what this represents?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is an image from the Kozluk mass grave exhumation. I'm familiar with this image and also the autopsy report and related evidence reports in relation to this body. You can see, from this image, that the man's hand is grasping the stems of a bush. When this grave was exhumed, the man was found to be holding that bush still, and his hand had to be pried away from that bush. What that indicates is that he had to have been alive at that stage. It also indicated a time reference, because that bush - and I'm conscious of moving outside my area of expertise - grows in Bosnia at that time. But, effectively, it shows the man was alive when he grasped that bush. He was then covered up and buried, and the ICTY removed the soil and exposed that image.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you investigated primary graves, did you ever consider the possibility that bodies were brought to the primary graves rather than actually killed in situ; in other words, that they were not executed there?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. We certainly considered that issue; and, in fact, the primary graves at Ravnice and Glogova showed clear evidence that the bodies had been taken there and dumped there. It was -- it wasn't evidence that those individuals had been executed there; except in a sub-grave within Glogova 1, there was evidence of individuals having been tied up and executed in situ. That was 12 individuals. But the majority of the bodies in Ravnice 1 and 2 and Glogova 1 and 2 appeared to have been dumped into those graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when a grave is initially identified, what are some of the factors that indicate whether a grave has been disturbed or tampered with?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: When the grave is first examined, they, the experts, take meticulous care to reveal the layers of soil, and they strip away subsequent layers. It becomes evident, even to my layman's eyes, where there is a difference, a disturbance in the soil. You could see that quite clearly. On some mass graves which were undisturbed, there was a clear indication of the grave outline in fluid which had leaked from the bodies; and if that had been disturbed, it was clearly obvious. But the disturbance was also obvious in the way the bodies were presented, in parts that were missing. A secondary grave would be a grave in which there's a -- the bodies are more broken up, more entangled, and a predominance of body parts.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, turning back to Exhibit P01899.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: In light of what you were just saying, can you just explain indications of disturbance, as you saw them?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, in this image, it's quite clear that a section of the grave has been removed. A significant number of bodies have been missed or left behind, but you can see that the original surface layer has been cut into. So that must have happened after the grave was initially created and the bodies were placed on it. That significant section of grave, of soil matrix, of bodies and body parts, is not present in that image. It has been taken somewhere else, and that process created the secondary mass graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, turning to Exhibit P0674, ERN number X006-4514, page 35.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, have you seen these images before?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: These are images from the report by Professor Richard Wright. I'm very familiar with the report and the images, and I indicate that I was present when, if not all the photographs were taken, most of them were taken, and I'm familiar with what they depict.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you indicate for the Trial Chamber what they depict?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Particularly, the image on the left shows marks left in the base and sides of the grave. You can clearly see teeth marks from a machine, a bucketed, heavy machine. That's on the walls at the middle rear of the image. You can also see those same scrapings on the floor of the -- of the grave. They're actually compacted grey soil. This is the Glogova 1 mass grave. And if you look on the right-hand pane, the third pane, you can clearly see vehicle tracks, heavy machinery tracks, in the base of the grave or in the soil surrounding the grave. I saw numerous instances of these markings, and I saw the archaeologists as they revealed these markings and developed them so that they could be photographed in this manner.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And is there any indication of what kind of device had been used on the bodies or in the graves that you're seeing right here?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The imprints of the machine were so obvious and so easily measured and photographed. We established, through investigative measures, comparing the dimensions of the teeth, the bucket, the wheels, the dimension between the wheels, that it was a front-end loader or an excavating machine; and in one instance, it was identified as an Ult 220, "Ult" being a manufacturer's name, and all the characteristics of the Ult machine were represented in those markings within the grave.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And what is the effect of the removal process on the bodies in the primary graves and the evidence associated with those bodies?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: If you have a primary undisturbed mass grave, you remove the soil and you have predominantly complete bodies normally laid out in a pattern where you can easily discern the bodies. If those bodies are then broken up and removed from the grave, and transported over rough roads in the back of vehicles, trucks, and dumped into another pit, and then that pit is compacted around them, not only do you spread the human remains and evidence across two sites, you significantly disrupt the bodies, significantly delaying identification, cause of death, and any of the other investigative processes that we'd hope to gain evidence from. You, in doing so, very effectively delayed the exhumation of the bodies. It takes a great deal more time to exhume a secondary mass grave than an undisturbed primary mass grave.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the course of your work as an investigator in the exhumations project, did you have a chance to observe the majority of -- the gender of the majority of the victims in the graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, part of the process of examining the bodies, particularly at the mortuary, was to try to identify the gender, so I was present during those examinations and discussed them with the ICTY experts. Effectively, we were able to identify a single female in the collection of bodies at that time. So from all the bodies and body parts that we had, we had identified one female from the Konjevic Polje 1 mass grave.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And was it possible to determine the age of the victims in the gravesites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, the process at the mortuary was to try and identify the bodies and give them an age range. I'm aware that different methodology was used, and I had discussed that with the experts; but, effectively, they were able to place them into various age groups: Some quite young, 12 years of age and up; some quite old, in 80s and 90s. But from the information available, the majority of the victims were in the middle-age range, say 20 or 30 to 50. The majority of those bodies were in that range.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the graves that you investigated, can you briefly indicate what the main findings were regarding the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The main cause of death, as indicated by the pathologist and anthropologist, was gunshot injury, gunshot wounds. There were a significant number of cases where they could not determine cause of death. There were other smaller groups which had been defined as "blast injury," and others from blunt-force trauma. The majority, however, had been shot; and as I say, in a significant number, there was no cause of death ascertained.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And why was this? For the last part, why was no cause of death ascertained for a significant number?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: From my experience, viewing the remains and being present at the mortuary, on a number of occasions, significant parts of the body would be missing. The pathologist, therefore, could not give a definitive cause of death, if there wasn't life-threatening injury to other parts of the body. Also, it's evident to me that if an individual is shot and the bullet doesn't strike a bone, when we examine the skeleton, because the flesh has been removed, the track of that bullet is not visible. So it could be that the individual was shot in a soft-tissue area and not in a bone, and we couldn't see that. Again, I'm not a pathologist, but that was clearly evident to me in looking at the bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Okay. And, generally, how were you able to tell that the bodies were from 1995 and not from some other time?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: We, of course, relied on the creation date of the mass grave, that the graves had been created in July of 1995, or had been created thereafter in September and October 1995. So they couldn't pre-date 1995, in July. We also -- we also looked at identification material found amongst the bodies. We would find identifications indicating the individuals were from Srebrenica, and often we would find those identifications indicating the person was recorded as missing from Srebrenica in the ICRC Book of the Missing. There were also other links which indicated a strong connection to Srebrenica, and therefore the time, including Dutch newspapers from 1995, Dutch medical military rations, Dutch artifacts, as well as artifacts which linked individuals to Srebrenica itself or to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And, in fact, how were individuals linked as being from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: A number of items were located which had indications that they were connected to Srebrenica. I recall an artificial leg which was bound by a tape marked "Feros Srebrenica," which I know to be a factory in Potocari, in the Srebrenica area. I've visited that factory and seen the tape in that factory. Similarly, a group of photographs were bound together by that tape. We found, I think it was in the Zeleni Jadar mass grave, a watch, a commemorative watch, which had markings in the B/C/S language indicating Srebrenica, I think it was "Ten years, Srebrenica," and as I say, again indications of connection with the Dutch-Bat, or Dutch Battalion, at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can we please take a look at Exhibit P0622, page 66.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, can you comment on what this is, please?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is an image from one of the reports relating to the ICTY exhumation process, and it shows a set of prayer beads. It's one of the mortuary photographs, one of the evidentiary photographs, and it shows a prayer bead. Looking at the image, it's from Pilica, which is the Branjevo military farm. In each of the graves, or in a majority of the graves of the graves, we found similar items which had indicated an affiliation with the Muslim religion. We small copies of the Quran, Quranic verses, and items which were clearly linked to the Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can we also take a look at also P0622, but page 69.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, can you comment on what this is?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, this is an image from an ICTY expert report. In the top pane, you see what I know to be a [indiscernible], an identification document. It's again from the Branjevo military farm exhumation, and normally you can see that there's a photograph on the right-hand pane of the booklet; and on the left would include date of birth, place of birth, residence, and other details. Often, that would include the place Srebrenica or similar. The bottom pane shows some of the material which would be often collected from the bodies. The majority of the bodies had identifications, wallets, and personal photographs and paperwork. This image shows some of those things: A Red Cross letter and photographs and other material. This is a mortuary photograph showing how the evidence was processed, photographed, and documented as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to religious artifacts you had mentioned before, did you ever recover any religious artifacts which were not related to the Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did not recover any item which gave a clear indication of any other faith. Clearly, some faiths would use prayer beads. From our examination of those beads, there was nothing to indicate they were from any other religious except Muslim, Islam, and we found no other indications of any other religious affiliation.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Now, when an ID was retrieved from a grave, such as an ID we just saw, what was the next step you took in order to identify the body?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: If we found an identification on a body or on a body part, the body would be removed and processed. The body would be taken to the mortuary, examined by a pathologist/anthropologist, the clothing would be taken and cleaned, the body would be prepared for examination. Whilst that was happening, the artifacts located with the body, such as the license or identifications, it would be examined by scene-of-crime officers. That would give us an indication of perhaps the identification of that individual. However, many of the individuals carried more than one identification. It was apparent to me that they had collected other identifications. I can surmise why. But that process then continued with an examination of the postmortem records, trying to match them against the identification document, and antemortem records provided by the family, which may assist in identifying that individual. The identification documents were really just a guide to try to identify the individuals from the physical characteristics at that stage of the bodies. At that stage, DNA was not heavily used.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: So do you know how many persons were actually identified on the basis of ID or in a forensic manner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the form of the question because I'm not sure whether if the question goes to one specific side or all sides, number one. And, number two, the last answer had to do with DNA, which was utilised only by the ICMP and the BCMP; and as part of your earlier rulings, that evidence would not be admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish to comment, Ms. Soljan? Thank you, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was no reference to expertise. He simply mentioned the word "DNA." And, furthermore, I can reinstate my question so as to specify the graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. I think the first point by Mr. Meek is a very valid one. The second one, I don't know where he got it from, but let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: From the ICTY-exhumed graves, how many forensic identifications were made on the basis of ID or any other forensic data or evidence?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I believe up to the time I gave evidence in the Blagojevic-Jokic trial, it would have been less than 100 for all the graves. It was a very low number of identifications which had been made from presumptive identifications based on physical characteristics. And to indicate to the Chamber, there was some DNA analysis conducted by the ICTY and by the Physicians for Human Rights, the PHR organisation. So part of that grouping of identifications also relied on DNA examinations, but predominantly there were very few identifications possible or made up until the process initiated by ICMP.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And based on your experience, could you tell why it would have been so difficult?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I indicated before that many of the individuals had multiple identifications. The family's information in relation to the bodies, if the individual had a wooden leg or an artificial leg, then that would significantly narrow it down. So the families would provide a description of stature or physical features and even clothing, but often that wasn't sufficient in any manner to narrow down the search. It was also made more difficult because the bodies had been broken up. It was very difficult to identify a torso and a set of legs or a part of an individual where you couldn't establish how tall that person was or how big that person was or if they did have an injury to an arm or a bone. Effectively, the breaking up of the bodies and the deterioration of the clothing and the physical artifacts significantly delayed any identification, not using a more definitive method such as DNA.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: At the time you testified in Blagojevic, what was the number of individuals found or exhumed from graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Based on the estimates by Jose Pablo Baraybar, it was, from all the graves that we had exhumed and examined the bodies, 2.570. I'm certain that's the correct number, but it may be necessary to check my records, but 2.570.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go into more detail in this report and the data regarding the individuals or the number of individuals exhumed. Just generally still, can you tell us whether there had been any evidence in any other graves that you'd exhumed that the -- that there were soldiers commingled with civilians inside the graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: We didn't find any significant number of uniforms to indicate military forces. We also did not find equipment in -- to indicate military forces. We did find some material and some very limited numbers of, say, a camouflage shirt or a military jacket. No, to my recollection or knowledge, no individuals were found in a complete uniform. One pistol was located in the belt of an individual at Glogova. He wasn't wearing military clothing, and that pistol was in a loaded condition. I understand a grenade was found in 1996 in the sleeve of an individual. But apart from that, we did not find evidence of military artifacts or clothing amongst the dead.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to the linkage of primary to secondary graves, what factors go into making this identification or this linkage?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you restate the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: I could. How were connections between primary and secondary graves determined forensically?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It was part of the process to see if the graves were, indeed, connected. We could see that they had been exhumed, a primary grave had been opened and the contents taken, and we had secondary graves. Initially, there were indications from physical artifacts, such as broken green glass present in the primary grave and present in the secondary grave, but not in the area around the grave; shell cases, an examination of shell cases to match the weapon that had fired them from the primary to the secondary grave; and also an examination of the soil samples within the primary grave and the secondary grave, as well as specific artifacts that were obviously connected.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Are there any other methods for identifying connections between graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: If you found part of an individual in a primary grave and part of an individual in a secondary grave, the same individual, and you could prove that that person was a whole body at one stage, clearly that would be a link that part of the body was in the primary grave, part of the body was in the secondary grave; a very strong link.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Okay. And have you, yourself, analysed all these various manners of identification of primary-to-secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I have, and I was involved in the process of collecting the evidence, of dealing with the experts, such as Dr. Tony Brown, in connecting soil samples and taking him to various locations, and also in providing him information. I also collected and examined the green glass fragments and the bottle labels from Kozluk and Cancari, as well as a very detailed examination of the Kravica warehouse, the Ravnice 1 and 2 and Glogova 1 and 2 mass graves, and the physical connections between those sites, as well as the Zeleni Jadar secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And so one of the methods used for identifying the connection between graves that you mentioned was blindfolds and ligatures. How were they used to determine this connection?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are a number of cloth blindfolds located within the graves, as well as cloth ligatures. They were all collected and examined, and I, along with others, conveyed those cloth blindfolds and ligatures to the Netherlands Forensic Institute where Dr. Susie Maljaars examined those cloth pieces, and she was able to group them into groupings that were very similar, that were indistinguishable from each other. It was obvious to me that there was a great similarity between the cloth blindfolds and ligatures. She, using a scientific examination of the cloth, the colour of the weave, the fabric, the density, et cetera, was able to show that many of the cloth ligatures represented in the primary grave were exactly the same as cloth ligatures and blindfolds represented in the secondary graves. Therefore, there was a strong connection between the blindfolds which had originally been in the primary grave and then had been transported to the secondary grave.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can we get Exhibit P00649. This would be page 15, or ERN 0095-0917.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, can you comment on what this is?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a page from a report that I produced. It indicates the result of Ms. Maljaars' examination of those cloth blindfolds and ligatures. When she returned to report to us, the items were identified by the Netherlands Forensic Institute numbers. I then matched those numbers with the numbers that we knew them; by, and then, using her report, I produced this chart which showed the links that she had identified. In the top of the image, the Branjevo military farm primary mass grave is linked to the Cancari Road 12 and Cancari Road 3 secondary grave. The Graboski [phoen] School, where a number of blindfolds were located, is matched to Hodzici 4, and Orahovac-Lazete 2 is matched to Hodzici 4, 5, and 3. There's also an indication of a match between Hodzici 4 and Liplje 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just turning back to the actual manner in which the ligatures and blindfolds were obtained, what was the protocol for handling the blindfolds and ligatures? What happened to them once they were identified?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: During the exhumation process, the blindfolds particularly identified on the heads of individuals, or close by the individuals, and the ligatures would be normally still present on the wrist, those items would be collected up with the body when it was exhumed, placed in the body-bag, photographed and recorded at the site, then conveyed to the mortuary at Visoko, where they would be again photographed. They would be then examined by the pathologist in situ, if possible. I saw that a number of the blindfolds had holes in them, which corresponded to injuries to the skull of the individual. They would examine them and the body. They would then be removed from the body, cleaned, examined, recorded, photographed, treated as evidence; and then they would be ultimately returned to The Hague, where we conveyed them to the Netherlands Forensic Institute for examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to examine all the blindfolds identified in the exhumation process, ICTY exhumation process, yourself?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: As part of my preparation for giving evidence and producing a report, I examined every physical artefact and photograph produced by the exhumation process, including every blindfold and every ligature. I examined them physically. I examined the associated records, including the photographic logs, the autopsy reports, the field notes, and the photographic logs and photographs of those images. I went through trying to identify what was a blindfold, what was a ligature. And because of the movement of the material within the grave, some of those items would slip off or become disassociated from the body, and I would examine those with the intention of establishing whether they could be considered blindfolds and ligatures. In that process, I discounted a large number of blindfolds and ligatures which were either damaged to the point where we couldn't confirm that they were blindfolds and ligatures, or there was a significant gap in the recording of where they were located and how they were processed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Could we please get Exhibit P02994. It's ERN X016-7719, page 12 for e-court purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you indicate to us what this is, Mr. Manning, please?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a table from my report previously presented to the trial. It relates to the primary and secondary mass graves. I created the table, and I based the figures on information that I had sought from either ICTY expert reports, our own internal information, or data collected from the exhumation/autopsy process. It shows the graves, the designations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President. Thank you very much. I would just like to know if we are again staying with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: ICTY?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- ICTY reports only; if not, I would just like to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you please put that question to the witness, and then we'll break and continue on this document afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, this chart, what specific exhumation process -- or when was it created?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It was created prior to my dealings with ICMP. The information I referred to and contained is all from ICTY expert reports and my examination of the records held by the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have the break now, and we will continue afterwards. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, has Mr. Kanguri [phoen] arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I am told he has made it, and he's in good spirits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I perhaps save some time on some issues? Ms. Soljan is about to go into some DNA results. It's my understanding that these are the same kind of results that came in under Mr. Brunborg, but they are just more updated. Now, that may run into your ruling a bit, because I don't know if you've determined it's DNA results. It's, you know, based on expert work, but it's the same material we relied on with Helge, and we were hoping not to bring in the DNA expert and how they did their DNA and all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But what's the witness supposed to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, as you'll find out, he fits it into his -- I think, as you can see, he's dealt with anthropology science to determine minimum numbers, and now he is assisted by the DNA results from minimum number of individuals. He'll explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's play it by the ear as we go along, and we'll see how far we can go on that. Ms. Soljan, have you finished with the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. No, because I saw it disappear from the screen. Okay. We have it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: If I could point your attention to the two columns stating "Blindfolds" and "Ligatures," could you please comment on those columns?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, those columns represent an account of the blindfolds and ligatures which I had conducted by examining the material. I have set that out in two columns, one to show the blindfolds, where they were located; and one to show the ligatures and in which mass graves they were located; and then they're simply totalled at the bottom of the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Okay. And what is the total number of blindfolds that have been located via ICTY exhumations?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: 448 blindfolds in total.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could we please get Exhibit P0265/99, page 91 -- 99.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you indicate what this is, please?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is an image taken at the Visoko mortuary, and you can see the body-bag in the background. It's of an individual who has code named "LZ2B41"; that is, Body 41 from the Lazete-Orahovac 2 primary mass grave. Very clearly, you can see across the victim's eyes a blindfold, a cloth blindfold. This is one of the blindfolds that was examined by Ms. Maljaars and myself, and it is very typical of the type of blindfold used; the colour, the width, the weave, the pattern, and that similarity is what was used to connect some of the primary to secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: If we could go back to Exhibit P02994, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Now, can you comment specifically on the ratio, or not the ratio, but what you found to be characteristic of graves -- blindfolds and where the blindfolds were found in the largest numbers?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you look at the table relating to blindfolds, a very significant number were found at Orahovac 1 and 2. From evidence presented to this Chamber, those two executions and graves were occurring at the same time; and for this exercise, I would treat them as the same or very similar incidents. So there's a lot of blindfolds at Orahovac 1 and 2. And if you see that Hodzici 3 and 4 also have a significant number of blindfolds when you consider that they are secondary graves. Orahovac-Lazete 2, again you see you see Hodzici Road 5 has a significant number of blindfolds. In Kozluk and its related secondary graves, a number of blindfolds are located in Kozluk, and a correspondingly high number of blindfolds located in a related secondary grave. I think that shows a pattern that matches up those two graves or those two types of graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And was that represented on the map as one of the factors linking the Orahovac to Hodzici graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Effectively, yes. It predominantly was based on Ms. Maljaars' work, showing the direct links, but you can also see that numerically it's also reflective of a connection between those two graves or two types of graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. And moving on to the next column, the column titled "Ligatures," can you briefly take us through that column also?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, it's an account of ligatures. You can see the majority of ligatures were found at the Kozluk primary mass grave. Again, a high number of ligatures were found at the secondary mass grave, Cancari Road 3. The next higher was at Branjevo military farm with a consistently high number at the secondary grave. The Cerska understood primary grave had 48 of the 150 individuals were bound. And in the Nova Kasaba 96 grave, 27 of the 33 individuals were also bound. In those two sets of graves, the binding was wire, predominantly steel or steel and plastic-coated wire, where the majority of the other graves were cloth or string or rope.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can we look at Exhibit P02063, page 118.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, can you indicate what this photograph represents and from which -- what grave it represents?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a mortuary photograph again. It is a part of an individual from Kozluk 3 primary mass grave. It's marked as "Body 719". You can clearly see the cloth ligature around the wrist of the individual. The other arm or wrist of the individual is not visible, but you can see the loop which would have gone through the wrist -- or gone around the wrist, I'm sorry. My examination of these ligatures showed that they would normally be looped around the wrist several times and then tied quite tightly. You can see in this image that the loop has been expanded out, if you like. So it was probably a double loop before the photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can we go on to Exhibit P02066, page 86.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This image shows those wire ligatures I was discussing. This is the person's hands tied behind his back. You can see his coat, his clothing. The wire ligatures in this instance was clearly very; tight, and on removal, you could see again that double loop for the wrists. Sometimes they were bound in two loops around the wrist and then tied off, various combinations, but this is an example of a wire ligature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And moving on to Exhibit P02066, page 61.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This image is another mortuary photograph. It shows a ligature taken from a Nova Kasaba 96 body. It's Nova Kasaba Sub-grave 2, Body 4, and it's Item 1 taken from that body, and it's a wire ligature. It's a plastic-coated wire similar to speaker wire; and, again, it formed loops around the wrists of the individual.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, Exhibits 2063, 2064 -- well, beginning with P02063, 2064, 2065, and 2066, all contain -- are binders of photographers of ligatures. Again, in the interest of time, I don't propose that we go through the blindfolds and ligatures, but I do intend to also tender them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do any of the Defence teams want to know exactly which documents Ms. Soljan is referring to, or can we proceed? Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, besides using the ligatures and the blindfolds as a manner for establishing the link between primary and secondary graves, was there any other significance to the location of blindfolds and ligatures?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Soljan. I don't think I understood the question. I think it's my fault.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: I will rephrase it. What does -- the fact that a body has ligatures or blindfolds on it, what does that indicate in the process of the investigations?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: My apologies. Clearly, the bodies that were ligatured and blindfolded, and in many cases they were both, both bound and blindfolded, is a clear indication that they were murdered. And as I said before, a number of the blindfolds had what was clearly bullet wounds through the material and into the head of the victim. These were people who were murdered.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you'd also indicated that another method --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could you please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: You had also indicated that another method of linking primary to secondary graves was through shell casings. Can you briefly explain how this was done? Did you participate in the collection and gathering of the shell cases, first of all?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours. I collected shell cases both from the mass graves and the collection at the Visoko mortuary. I was also involved in having them shipped to the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Fire-arms Agency in the United States for examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And were you able to link primary and secondary graves based on the shell casings?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. We were able to link the primary and secondary graves. I'm familiar with this process and have used it previously to coming to the ICTY, but I'm not a ballistics expert. However, the markings on the shell cases, when they are ejected from a weapon, are unique. They can be examined under microscope. They were examined by the ATF and shown -- some shell cases were shown to be fired by the same weapon, although they were in separate graves; that is, a primary and a secondary grave. So either the same weapon was fired at the primary grave and then again fired at the secondary grave, or the shell cases were collected from the primary grave and conveyed to the secondary grave. And on examination at the ATF, they produced a report which they forwarded to myself, and I examined that report and produced a table in relation to the findings from that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit P00 -- sorry, P01912.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an image from the Kozluk mass grave. It shows a body. I believe it to be Body 501. The body is blindfolded, and the posture of the body indicates that it was also bound. But more importantly, you can see in the foreground, just near the arm, a shell case, a 7.62 shell case. That is the sort of material that we would find in the grave, in this case the primary grave. We would find that material in the secondary grave, collect them, process them, and then they would be compared by the ATF.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And for the record, Mr. Manning, could you just indicate where the shell casing is located in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: If you look at the middle, perhaps left, of the image, below the arm of the body is a cylindrical object, and it's facing, say, from -- diagonally across the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, going back to Exhibit P00648.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you please indicate for the Trial Chamber what this chart represents?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a chart I produced for one of my reports. It is based on the work of Martin Als [phoen] from the ATF, and it essentially shows where a shell case was located in more than one location. At the top of the diagram, Kravica warehouse and Zeleni Jadar 5 indicates a shell case was found at the Kravica warehouse execution point. Another shell case was found at Zeleni Jadar 5 secondary mass grave, and that those shell cases were fired was from the same weapon. With the Cerska entry below that, it shows the Cerska grave; shell cases located within the grave; matched shell cases on the surface, on the roadway, and on the other side of the roadway. This is significant, in that there is evidence that individuals were shot at the gravesite at Cerska, and that's consistent with the shooting being -- taking place at the site. Below that is the Lazete or Orahovac gravesite, and again shell cases found at the gravesite are linked to shell cases found at the three secondary graves, Hodzici Road 3, 4, and 5. The dam surface, this is the Petkovci Dam, or the Dam at Petkovci. Shell cases found on the surface were also found within the grave. Kozluk primary mass grave, shell case found there matched the shell case found at the secondary Cancari Road 3 mass grave.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honours, this is Exhibit P00649 at page 16.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, you also indicated that green glass was another artefact or another manner of linking up primary and secondary graves. Can you briefly explain how this was done?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The primary mass grave at Kozluk was in a rubbish dump, the area next to the Drina River. Within and around that grave was a very significant amount of broken green glass bottle and bottling factory labels. It was effectively throughout the site. When we examined the related -- or the secondary mass grave of Cancari 3, we located green glass fragments within the grave, which were indistinguishable from those found at Kozluk; and, more importantly, there were no other green glass fragments around the area. So the only green glass fragments and bottle labels were found within the grave itself, forming a strong link to the Kozluk mass gravesite. I'd indicate that the bottle labels indicated the Vitinka bottle factory, which was a kilometre from the Kozluk mass gravesite.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can we take a look at Exhibit P02063 at page 218.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you comment on this image, Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a victim in a Kozluk mass grave. You can see the blindfold across the eyes. More importantly, in this process, you can see the broken green glass around the individual. It's somewhat difficult, given the colouration of this film, but the glass in the top right-hand corner and the glass to the left top, and also around the body, is broken green glass from bottles. As I say, it's unfortunate this image is a little bit blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And going on to the next image, P02063, page 25.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This shows, again, the mass grave with significant amount of broken green glass behind the body. You can see it's a rubbish dump, and that in this case the body is just up against that broken glass, which is, in fact, green.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And, finally, Exhibit P02063, page 36.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see quite clearly in this image the pieces of broken glass, particularly in the right top-hand corner and just near the arm of the body. You can see that it's fragmented green glass, and this was -- was so obvious within both graves, including the bottle factory labels, to provide a very positive link between the two graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, another factor that you had mentioned as linking primary and secondary graves is also soil and pollen analysis. Could you tell us a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The ICTY engaged Professor Tony Brown from the University of Exeter, who collected soil and pollen samples from the mass grave and surrounding the mass grave. On occasions, when he wasn't able to attend, the archaeology team collected samples for him from various parts of the grave, and he then examined those soil and pollen samples. And based on his work, I was able to provide a definitive link between the soil type that was in the primary grave and the soil type that was in the secondary graves, indicating that the soil type in the secondary grave was foreign to that area but was the same as the primary gravesite. I'd indicate I assisted Professor Brown significantly in his collection of soil samples and also in the preparation or the provision of data for his report relating to the mass graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And as a result of this analysis, does -- does this -- is this analysis reflected with respect to the graves depicted on this map?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. Where we had a positive soil sample link, I've indicated on the map. If you look at Kozluk and Cancari Roads 3 and 2, you see that I've indicated there to be a soil and pollen sample, which provides a link between those graves, and I've done that for the other graves as well, where a soil sample has been linked.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Manning, did you also examine evidence found at execution sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We collected evidence from the various execution points, particularly the Pilica Dom and the Kravica warehouse. I was very much involved in the examination of the Kravica warehouse. I was there several years whilst we were exhuming the Glogova 1 and 2 and Ravnice 1 and 2 graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: What type of evidence was collected? Let's begin with the Kravica warehouse. What type of evidence were you collecting at the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Prior to my commencing with the ICTY, the United States Naval Criminal Investigation Service had attended the Kravica warehouse and the Pilica Dom, and they had taken a large number of samples from the walls and ceiling of the buildings. These were samples of what appeared to be blood and tissue, and also what appeared to be explosive residue. As I say, they collected significant numbers of samples from both the warehouse and the Pilica Dom. They produced a report in relation to collection, and I conveyed the samples of blood and explosive to the in the Netherlands Forensic Institute and had dealings with staff there in relation to the examination of that material. They produced reports in relation to those examinations.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And besides blood samples and explosive residue samples, was there any other material collected or observed at the warehouse to indicate that there was a crime scene?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Particularly at the Kravica warehouse, there was clear evidence of blood and human hair on the walls of the warehouse. There was a very significant number of bullet strikes to the warehouse, both externally and internally. There were a number of grenade fly-off leaders, grenade release leaders, found outside the building. Initials examinations by Dr. Hagland had also found a significant, a small but significant, number of human skeletal remains, small pieces of bone. Also, on my examination of the warehouse, we collected parts of the structure of the warehouse; the walls, the panelling, the decorative concrete fins of the building.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And how were the walls significant to your investigation?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The walls of the warehouse are insulating foam sandwiched between concrete, and they're painted in different colours in different coats. We saw, within the Glogova 1 and 2, Ravnice 1 and 2, and Zeleni Jadar 5 and 6 graves, pieces of that construction, pieces of masonry with foam between the two concrete sides. We also saw pieces of the decorative fin of the building, and also pieces of the door frame and steel work within the building.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Was there anything else that you found at the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Significantly, the sign or one of the signs above a small door on the eastern side of the warehouse was a sign in Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian which was an advertising sign, and it was made from foam lettering which had been painted. A piece of that foam lettering, indistinguishable from the foam at the warehouse, was found at the Ravnice gravesite, and it was possible to see where that piece of foam fit into the existing damaged sign at the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can we take a look at Exhibit P001565.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you comment on this picture, Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is an image of the Kravica warehouse, looking from the roadway which runs from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac. It's taken in winter, and it's foreshortened because of the angle. But if you look at the right of the photo, down to the first small door in the middle of the image, that's the section of the warehouse that was specifically examined by the Naval Criminal Investigation Service and our subsequent examinations. The sign I was speaking of is above that door. You can see some writing above the first door there in the middle. If you move to the right of the image, there's two windows and then a very large opening. That was the front door, front gate, of the Kravica warehouse, and that is where the missing insulated wall and decorative fin and door frame was removed from the building and partially placed in the mass graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can we look at Exhibit P001568.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you comment on this image, please?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I recognise this to be an image of the Kravica warehouse interior. You're looking at the far wall from the large opening. You can see a window in the top right-hand corner, and I've examined this area in great detail, this building in great detail. You can clearly see blood, hair, and other tissue all on the walls and ceiling of this building, along with what looks like explosive residue and explosive patterns on the wall.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on to the investigations carried out at the Pilica Dom, can you briefly indicate what kind of evidence was collected there?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In the same manner, the Naval Criminal Investigation Service collected blood and tissue samples from the walls, the stage area, and the floor. The Pilica Dom is a community hall, and they also collected samples of explosive residue from areas which were clearly the seat of explosions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Let's take a look at Exhibit P001 -- P01811.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Can you please indicate what the photograph depicts?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This photographs shows the Pilica Dom. It's looking slightly to the side. The front of the building is to the left of the photograph, and the road, the main road, would be in front of the entrance there at the left of the image.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And Exhibit P00 -- P01817.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the interior of the Pilica Dom. You can see again blood and tissue on the walls. You can also see damage to the floor in a V-shaped pattern. This is believed to be the seat of an explosion, and that sort of area is where they collected the explosive residue traces from.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Did you review the reports which analysed both the Pilica Dom as well as the Kravica warehouse evidence, particularly regarding explosive residue?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And did you, yourself, have a chance to see these -- to see this evidence?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I physically examined the collection of the evidence that was collected by the Naval Criminal Investigation Service and then conveyed that to the Netherlands Forensic Institute; and, then, on completion of their examination, returned that evidence to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Manning, you have documented the results of the exhumations that the ICTY has participated in, have you not?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And can you tell us, how many reports in all have you prepared?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I prepared three major reports relating to the exhumation and autopsy process and the related scientific examinations of evidence. I also had prepared a statement presented in the Milosevic trial, the Srebrenica section of that, and I have produced a report in relation to the exhumations, which was just completed recently.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to the reports that you produced while you were still working at the ICTY, what type of information did you rely upon in preparing those reports?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: A significant amount of the information I gleaned from the examination and summary of the ICTY experts, but equally a large proportion of the information was gained by myself from an examination of the ICTY data and records or my examination of the physical artifacts, such as the blindfold and ligatures, such as the photographic and evidence collection notes in relation to exhibits and artifacts, the location of the mass graves, when and how long they're exhumed for. Basically, it was a combination of an examination of the expert reports and an examination of the data held by the Srebrenica team and myself.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And would you say that your review of expert data was consistent with what you were observing in the field?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Very much so. The reports were written by experts that I had dealt with and discussed through the process of exhumations, the findings, but also they were consistent with the evidence that we were finding in the artifacts and also corroborative of witness and survivor accounts.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And what types of data is contained in your reports that goes beyond expert reports; in other words, what would have been what just you personally would have seen or done?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, it's in relation to where the graves were, when they were exhumed, how long that process took, what artifacts were available to show the links between graves, how many blindfolds were located, where were they located, how many ligatures. Also, the identifications that had been located amongst the bodies had been examined, but no correlation of those identifications to the bodies in the graves had been made. I produced an annex which listed the identifications, what they were, where they were found. I also included an annex in relation to where religious artifacts were found and what those religious artifacts were. And, in a similar way, examining the photographs to identify artifacts which could assist in linking, and also I presented details of the examination of the Sevar [phoen] meadow suspected execution point, which I had conducted the examination with an archaeologist, and I presented those details in the report as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Now, would it be correct to say that in each one of the reports produced up until 2003, you also indicated the number of individuals found in the graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct. I also indicated the age and gender and other details taken from expert reports; but I indicated, in that report or those reports, the MNI, the minimal number of individuals, which was a calculation produced by significantly Jose Pablo Baraybar, the chief anthropologist for the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And could we go to Exhibit P02994, please, page 12.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: This is already a familiar image to you, Mr. Manning, but can you tell us, first of all, where this chart is from or where this chart is located?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, this is from my 2003 report. There's a previous version from another report which had the then current information. This was produced in one of my forensic reports for presentation to the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And can you clarify, explain what the total numbers under the columns "MNI (linked)" and "MNI (unlinked)" mean?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The numbers represented there were provided by Jose Pablo Baraybar; and, if you like, the MNI (linked) column is his calculation of the number of bodies, based on an anthropological assessment of bones that were present in each of the graves. It says "linked" because if you count the number of bones in a primary graves and then you count the number of bones in a secondary grave that are connected, you can have to count the bones together, and that's what he did. The next column shows the raw numbers, if you like, before he used his process of linking primary to secondary graves; and then they are totalled at the end.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: And as of 2003, how many identified bodies were there, therefore, in relation to the ICTY-conducted exhumations, or exhumations conducted between 1996 and 2001?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: At the time when I produced this table, we had identified, as in these were individuals not identified as a name, we had identified the remains of 2.570 individuals within all those primary and secondary mass graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, since this report, you have also created a new report. Can you tell us what the purpose of this report is?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Specifically, it was to give an update on the number of graves, when they had been exhumed, by whom, and provide a brief summary of all of the graves. Previously, my reports had indicated the graves that we knew of then. So part of the reason for doing the report was to show which graves had been exhumed, when and by whom, and the current state of knowledge in relation to those graves. The second part was to provide an updated number of the number of individuals or victims identified within those Srebrenica-related mass graves. I used data provided -- simple-number data provided by the ICMP, and produced a report and table detailing which graves had which numbers and a total of identified individuals or bodies or victims.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Was there any other basis for information contained in your report besides the ICMP data?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No. In fact, in creating the report, I had a bit of a quandary as to whether I should try and count different things. I decided I would only use the ICMP data, even though I'm aware that other identifications have been made outside the ICMP DNA data, that is, the presumptive IDs that were made early on, some of the ICTY DNA results, and identifications made in a presumptive manner by PHR. So, effectively, I knew that this number would be conservative and not include some numbers identified through another process. I took the view that I would only use one source of data, and that would be ICMP data provided to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: So the method by which you prepared your latest report is different as compared to the reports you had written previously?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: To a degree, in that I examined -- well, I took the data that they had and matched it to our primary mass graves, but in a very similar manner I did the same thing with the ICTY expert reports and the information provided by Jose Pablo Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: THE ICTY TEAM
utterances.text: Were there any particular skills required for the creation of this report, any expertise?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I don't know if it's correct to say "expertise." I think it's more correct to say "knowledge." I have probably a very deep knowledge of the graves and where they're located, and the data that supports that and behind that, but effectively it would have been relatively straightforward for someone else to go through the numbers and divide them up into the primary and secondary mass graves. The issues perhaps would be that I know them quite well and I know what the grid references and locations and what someone would expect to find from those graves; and the fact that Kozluk is actually three graves but we treated it as one, and it should be treated as such; and that Ravnice is two graves but should be treated as one. So, effectively it's my knowledge of the whole situation from 1996 until 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I'm not going into a new set of questions, and I think it may be more prudent to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. How much more time do you envisage your examination-in-chief requires?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not think more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right, so we'll reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of December, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
